newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka groups to petition courts over media bill.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka groups to petition courts over media bill.

text.p: Sri Lanka's main opposition party and media watchdog groups plan to petition the island's Supreme Court over a broadcast bill that is seen by opponents as an attempt to stifle freedom of speech.

The opposition United National Party (UNP), media groups and some members of the ruling People's Alliance have lambasted the bill, which seeks to set up a broadcasting authority with wide powers to monitor, regulate and grant operating licences to radio and television broadcasters.
UNP sources said on Monday the party was consulting lawyers to challenge the bill in the Supreme Court.
They said the bill, introduced in parliament last week, would be doomed if the Supreme Court ruled it needed two-thirds vote in parliament to pass.
The ruling People's Alliance, with a wafer-thin one-seat majority, would find it difficult to carry the bill if the court made a two-thirds vote mandatory.
"That will be the end of it (the bill)," one UNP leader said told Reuters.

The Free Media Movement, an independent media watchdog, said in a statement at the weekend that the government had gone back on its word to publish a white paper for public discussion before presenting the bill.
"The bill has been viewed as impinging on freedom of expression and also gives political authorities unrestricted control over the broadcast media," the statement said.
Officials with the movement, who declined to be quoted, said both their organisation and the Editors' Guild also planned to challenge the bill in the Supreme Court.

The bill calls for annual renewal of licences with backing from the authority's board of directors. The board will consist of secretaries to the various government ministries, including the defence ministry.

The bill has also been criticised by the Sri Lanka Muslim Congress (SLMC) and Democratic United National (Lalith) Front (DUNLF), two key constitutents of the People's Alliance which have said they will make all efforts to ensure the government does not suppress media freedom.
"Enacting such a repressive piece of legislation violates the true spirit of a free media," DUNLF legislator Ravi Karuanayake was quoted as saying by the Sunday Leader newspaper.
The UNP last week objected to the inclusion of the defence secretary in the proposed authority's board of directors, saying the military's growing role was a cause of concern.

Sri Lanka's security-conscious government, which is fighting a separatist war with minority Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels, has previously warned private radio and television stations against broadcasting news that could create ethnic disharmony.
Sri Lanka currently has eight television stations -- all but two owned by the government -- and about a dozen radio stations, most of them privately owned.
